summary.text:
A 10-page standalone Treasury Management Strategy for 2026/27 from a small Hertfordshire district. The distinctive shape: zero PWLB debt, zero long-term borrowing of any kind. Broxbourne's entire £51.65m debt portfolio is short-dated inter-local-authority money at 4.15%-4.65%, matures April-September 2026, and is due to be refinanced in the same market. Investments £53m at 31 December 2025 (falling to a forecast £51m by 31 March 2027 as the capital programme is drawn down). The paper delegates every balance-sheet number — CFR, affordable borrowing limit, operational boundary — to the separate Capital Strategy 2026/27, which is not read in this session.

The loan-book reconciliation ties at zero: the paper prints £0 long-term borrowing at page 1; our PWLB file holds no borrower for Broxbourne under any variant of the name (only BROXTOWE, a Nottinghamshire district, appears in the file). The balance-sheet identity cannot be checked from this paper alone because CFR, other long-term liabilities and internal borrowing are not quantified — the paper describes the position qualitatively as "under-borrowed" but does not size it.

The strongest testable statement in the paper is at page 3: 2-to-5-year borrowing will be considered where rates fall below 4%. At the paper's reference date (22 December 2025) the 5-year certainty rate was 4.81%, 0.81pp above the trigger. Yesterday afternoon (14 August 2026, DMO notice 314/26 PM) it was 5.34%, 1.34pp above the trigger — the curve moved further from the trigger, not closer. MUFG's forecast in the paper had 5Y falling to 4.30% by September 2026 and 4.10% by March 2027; the direction has been the opposite.

The 2026/27 budget shows a near-matched treasury position: £2,310,000 of investment income at 3.84% against £2,299,617 of debt interest at an implied 4.45% — net income of £10,383, essentially net-zero. That is the shape of a small council using its own cash to fund an under-borrowed CFR while funding external debt from a short-term inter-authority market that clears close to Bank Rate.

First-contact fit is weak. There is no PWLB position for us to price, no CFR to reconcile against, no forward treasury committee date published in this paper, and no officer email address on the front sheet or in the report author line ("Democratic Services" only). The Cabinet meeting the paper was written for is six months past. A draft is written on the 4% trigger and the shape of the book, but it is a general first-contact rather than a paper-tied one, and it has no address to send to.

officer.body:
Dear Colleague,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep the data relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, and yours landed for the 10 February Cabinet. Below are a couple of thoughts, six months on. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

One thing worth saying upfront. Our loan file holds no PWLB debt for Broxbourne, which matches the £0 long-term borrowing at the top of your page 1 table. Your whole £51.65m debt portfolio is short-dated inter-authority money, priced against a market we don't publish. So the things below are the ones your own paper opens up, not a reconciliation of a book we hold.

Your paragraph on borrowing strategy sets a testable line: longer-term borrowing options of 2 to 5 years will be considered where rates fall below 4%. At the time of the paper the 5-year Certainty rate was 4.81%. Yesterday's afternoon fix (DMO notice 314/26 PM, 14 August 2026) was 5.34% — the 5-year moved further from your trigger, not closer, over the six months since. MUFG's forecast in the paper had it at 4.30% by September and 4.10% by March 2027; the direction it took is the one it took. No suggestion attached — the trigger is your line and where the curve sits is a fact.

The other thing worth noting is the shape of the book. Your paragraph 2 says the £51.65m matures between April and September 2026, all of it, financed principally by other local authorities. By yesterday most of that refinancing window has passed. Nothing published since February tells us what you rolled into and we aren't asking. Of the councils we've read this year almost all use inter-authority short-term for part of a portfolio; Broxbourne's is the shape where it is essentially the whole portfolio. That is a distinct position and it moves with Bank Rate, which was 3.75% at your paper and still sits there.

One standing point, added not for Broxbourne specifically but because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151. The liability benchmark — a projection of what a council's external debt would need to be to leave a minimum cash cushion — becomes central. For a book that is 100% short-dated and 100% counterparty-market, the pathway that comes out of it is the useful artefact for deciding when and whether to lengthen. You can see the shape of what every council we've read holds today at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On training, three fit the paper. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets covers the sole market your portfolio uses. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice picks up the point above. Liquidity & cashflow forecasting is the discipline that makes a 100%-short-dated book workable. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/
